  • Note: The reading ma-ah-ri-ša follows [RN435: 60], who take am as the ventive particle (i-kab-ba-sa-am). It seems more likely that it is the preposition ana. [RN2720: 324a] (and [RN7444: 425 fn. 1] and [soden1978erste: 92] and ) read the line as i-kab-ba-sa-am-ma ih-ri-ša, from ḫarāšu(um) I “im Kindbett liegen” (“…und legte sich ins Kindbett,” the subject being the birth-goddesses). This reading is ruled out by [RN1445: 158] on the basis of SB III 18 (āšib mahrīš[a]); see also the arguments in favor of -sa-am ma-ah- by [RN744: 113 fn. 23] and [RN603: 57 fn. 96].

32

  • N: [ṭi]ṭṭa | ibāl | ... [ ... ]
  • T: She prayed to the clay … […]
  • L: [ṭi]ṭṭa ← ṭīdu I “clay, mud for bricks, mortar, plaster”; ibāl ← bâlu I “to supplicate”
  • Note: As understood here, Māmi recites a Kultmittelbeschwörung to the clay and the oil she uses in the ritual. See [fromebllab0037: 79]: “These two verses probably form a parallel couplet. At the beginning of the verse, the restoration follows K.7816 o 14’ (= SB II 25), which reads: [ṭi-i]ṭ-ṭa i-kab-ba-sa-am ma-ah-ri-ša. Note, however, that the spelling [ṭi]-ṭa differs from the spelling in line 14’. The goddess Mami seems to mix here oil in order to awake the first sexual desire among humans, as attested in some nīš libbi texts, where ointments made from a mixture of animal, vegetable, and mineral ingredients are applied onto the genitals of both men and women to rekindle sexual desire ([zisa2022the: 181-183]); it could also be an allusion to the anointing with oil that took place as a betrothal rite, and which in some magical texts is also performed on figurines ([malul1988studies: 161-179]; [RN2805xs: 139]).”
NinNA1 o ii 30'. [ṭi?]-ṭa# i-ba-li# a-x [x x] x [x x x x (x)]

35

  • N: zikaru [ ( ... ) ] | ana eṭ[li ( ... ) ]
  • T: “Let the male (baby) [turn] into a young man,
  • L: zikaru ← zikaru I “male, virile stat. is manly”; ana ← ana I “(aš-š... etc.) to, for (freq. abbr. an, with assimilation of n…”; eṭ[li ← eṭlu I “manly”
  • Note: See [fromebllab0037: 80]: “@url{/fragmentarium/K.3399}{K.3399} (Ms. S in [RN435]), which preserves the Neo-Assyrian recension of the epic, can be partially corrected thanks to the present manuscript. See in particular @url{/fragmentarium/K.3399}{K.3399} iii 21’ (NA c+26 in the eBL edition), previously reconstructed as [z]i-ka-ru a#-na# [ardati] ([RN435: 62]). @url{/fragmentarium/K.3399}{K.3399} iii 22’ (NA c+27 in the eBL edition), previously read [x] x el-li x [x] ([RN435: 62]), should be read as [ana K]I.SIKIL li-x [(x) x x x x]. The verb after ardati is perhaps “to become” or “to change into” (târu, ewû), as in @url{/corpus/L/1/4/OB/II}{Gilgameš OB II} 108-109: šamnam iptašaš-ma awīliš īwe, “he anointed himself with oil and became a man”. The traces preserved in the parallel line in @url{/fragmentarium/K.3399}{K.3399} could be reconciled with li-be#, perhaps a NA form of līme/līwe ([RN27201: §21d]). Manuscript @url{/fragmentarium/K.4539}{K.4539} + @url{/fragmentarium/K.5902}{K.5902}, l. 7’ seems to preserve a few traces before SI, perhaps reconcilable with the end of ME. In this passage, the male and female babies created in the preceding lines of the epic “become” a young man (eṭlu) and a young woman (ardatu), respectively, i.e. they become ready for sexual intercourse [Regarding the parallel passage found in the Old Babylonian version of the poem, compare also the interpretation provided by [vonsoden1991urmensch: 48-49], who suggested that this creation myth involved an androgynous creature from which humanity would originate: von Soden believes that the eṭemmu mentioned in OB I 215 (ina šīr ilim (w)eṭemmu(m) libši, [RN435: 58-59]) was androgynous, later divided in half by a deity, in order to create man and woman. To support his hypothesis, von Soden refers to other mythologies, citing, for example, the myth of androgynes in Plato. Since the passage is fragmentary, von Soden’s interpretation remains higly speculative. On the connection between youth and sexual vigor in Mesopotamian texts, see [zisa2022the: 131-135].].”
NinNA1 o ii 33'. zi-ka-ru a-na eṭ#-[li]

  • N: lilqe | a[rd]ata | kuzubš[a]
  • T: “May he take in the maiden’s charms!

  • Note: See [fromebllab0037: 80]: “The OB MS (@url{/fragmentarium/BM.92608}{BM 92608} = CT 46 no. 4) reads probably [... ku-z]u-u[b-ša] (rev. iv 1’). The phrase kuzba(m) leqû is an expression that indicates sexual attraction ([RN3091: 32]), as in @url{/corpus/L/1/4/SB/I}{Gilgameš SB I} 178: ūrki pitê-ma kuzubki lilqe, “bare your sex so he may take in your charms!”, (cp. also SB I 187). Another meaning of kuzba(m) leqû, attested in incantations (e.g., @url{/corpus/Mag/1/1/SB/III}{Maqlû III 10}, see [RN2544: 303]; cp. [zisa2022the: 133]), is “to deprive a woman of her attractiveness”, which seems unlikely in our context. The line contains a σχῆμα καθ’ ὅλον καὶ μέρος (“the maiden (and) her charm”), a figure frequently used in Atramḫasīs (see [RN1778]).”
